summary: Oxyfedrine is a partial beta-adrenergic agonist and coronary vasodilator used historically for angina pectoris, coronary insufficiency and ischemic heart disease. It increases coronary blood flow and improves myocardial oxygen supply with a mild positive inotropic effect. It is NOT FDA-approved (never approved in the US; reportedly marketed mainly in India). It inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, so a disulfiram-like reaction can occur with alcohol. Data derive from European/international pharmacology references; several detailed clinical fields are not authoritatively sourced.

moa: Oxyfedrine acts as a partial agonist at beta-adrenoceptors (beta-1 and beta-2). It reduces coronary vascular tone (coronary vasodilation), improves myocardial metabolism and increases coronary blood flow to both normal and ischemic myocardium, improving myocardial oxygen supply, with a mild positive inotropic/chronotropic effect. An indirect sympathomimetic component arises from its active metabolite norephedrine. Oxyfedrine is also a covalent inhibitor of aldehyde dehydrogenase, which underlies a potential disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.

relative: Conditions where increased cardiac stimulation is undesirable (e.g., tachyarrhythmia, severe hypertension, hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma) - expected class-based cautions for a beta-agonist
Significant aortic outflow obstruction / altered flow states

preg: Adequate safety data in pregnancy have not been established. As a sympathomimetic agent, use only if clearly needed; a formal pregnancy category is not authoritatively documented.
lact: No data are available on use during breastfeeding; exercise caution and weigh benefit against potential risk.
renal: About 90% of active metabolites are renally excreted, so caution is reasonable in significant renal impairment; specific dose-adjustment guidance is not established.
hepatic: Oxyfedrine is extensively hepatically metabolized; use with caution in hepatic impairment. Specific dose-adjustment guidance is not established.

major: Alcohol - oxyfedrine inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, so a disulfiram-like reaction (flushing, nausea, palpitations, tachycardia, hypotension) can occur
moderate: Beta-adrenergic blockers (e.g., propranolol) - antagonize the beta-adrenergic effects of oxyfedrine
interactions.food: No clinically significant food interaction described.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - a disulfiram-like alcohol-intolerance reaction is mechanistically expected because oxyfedrine inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase.

monitoring: Signs of an alcohol-intolerance reaction if alcohol is taken
counsel: Take exactly as prescribed, usually three times daily
Avoid alcohol - it can cause flushing, nausea, palpitations and a fall in blood pressure
Report palpitations, tremor or worsening chest pain
Tell your clinician about other heart medicines, especially beta-blockers
pk: Store at room temperature per manufacturer
pearls: NOT FDA-approved - never approved in the US; reportedly marketed mainly in India. Data from European/international pharmacology references
Partial beta-adrenergic agonist that increases coronary blood flow rather than reducing oxygen demand like beta-blockers
Inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase - warn patients about a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol
Oral bioavailability ~85%; extensively metabolized to the active metabolite norephedrine (~75-100% of dose), ~90% of metabolites renally excreted
missed: No specific missed-dose instruction is documented. General guidance: take the missed dose when remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip it; do not double the dose.
overdose: Overdose data are not specifically documented; exaggerated sympathomimetic effects (tachyarrhythmia, palpitations, tremor, hypertension) would be expected. Management is supportive; a beta-blocker may be considered for severe tachyarrhythmia.
